Title: Play to Lose/Self-oust vs Play to Win case study

Messages.Author: Jeff Kuta
Messages.Body:
Situation:
A (ousted) > B > C > D > E

B has 3x fighty but weakened !Tremere
C has 3x relatively healthy, untapped !Brujah, Dogs of War and vote
lock
D has 5x Daughters and can push votes through sometimes
E has 8x Independent childer of Mata Hari and 1 VP

B has 5 pool
C has 1 pool but 3-5 after his next turn via Dolls/bloat
D has 10+ pool
E has 12+ pool

B announces to the table that he sees no hope and transfers down to 1
pool.
C asks if this means he is transferring out and therefore won't
interfere with his turn.
B denies this and says he's trying to force the issue for C and D to
do something to alter the game state.

So what's really going on here? Most would interpret transferring down
to 1 pool as intent to self-oust from a hopeless situation. However, B
has some permanent and transient intercept available. So
theoretically, he might do some blocking, or perhaps bounce some of
the horde of bleeds for 1 which are coming his way on E's next turn.
But if it really isn't so hopeless, why transfer down to 1 pool?

I guess my big picture question is this: Is it legal to put yourself
into an extremely fragile position (which is just shy of transferring
out of a hopeless situation) and still try to interfere with the game?
Where do you draw the line between choosing how you lose the game and
choosing how to take others down with you? While I believe this
situation is unusual, it would be bad for the game if this sort of
brinksmanship became the norm for winning a close game (e.g. Transfer
down to an almost untenable position, than twist arms to get me out of
my own predicament). Any additional guidance is appreciated.

Jeff

Can't say really... But to be honest, in his position might be worse
then you think. Did B try to take actions/no actions to survive only
to have C hurt his vampires? Did player A and Player C do so much
hurting on his minions that he can't mount an effective defence
anymore, but player C is still worried and rushing/hurting backwards?
Is D so worried about C that he's not putting forward pressure, con
booning only himself, or even hurting player B for some reason? From
the sounds of it C is worried about B, leaving 3 untap minions. Since
B couldn't oust C right then at 1 pool, B probably won't get another
chance to take out C before he's gone. His best bet to survive is to
have the other player kill/cripple his predator, and if he can't ask
for it... Force their hand into it. In this example, 5 pool vs 1 pool
might just mean that E bleed with all 8 minon instead of 4.

If it isn't "really hopeless" and B has some reasonable chance of possibly
getting more VPs, then this violates play to win.

> I guess my big picture question is this: Is it legal to put yourself
> into an extremely fragile position (which is just shy of transferring
> out of a hopeless situation) and still try to interfere with the game?

If "putting yourself in a fragile situation" doesn't violate play to win, then yes.

> Where do you draw the line between choosing how you lose the game and
> choosing how to take others down with you? While I believe this

You don't. There is no line to draw. Being able to choose how you gt your
remaining zero VPs is exactly the same as choosing how to take others down with
your (or elevate them -- the normal term is "king making").

> situation is unusual, it would be bad for the game if this sort of
> brinksmanship became the norm for winning a close game (e.g. Transfer
> down to an almost untenable position, than twist arms to get me out of
> my own predicament). Any additional guidance is appreciated.

It is illegal to take yourself down from a position of "can reasonably get more
VPs" to "cannot reasonable get more VPs". Other than that, the "tactic" or going
from zero VPs to zero VPs (no change) in order to get a king making position
(still no change) and pointing out your zero VP status (no change) in the hopes
of making a deal for more VPs is fine.

How about this situation (happened to me in the last tournament I
played):

I was playing a combat rush/bleed deck. My prey was playing a large
capacity voting/bloat deck. I pull out a minion, my prey pulls out
Arika. I rush and torporise Arika before my prey has a chance to
minion tap her, and pull out my second minion. My prey decides that
there is nothing that can be done, and just gives up. No more
transfers, no asking for a rescue, nothing. Just sits there waiting
for me to bleed through the 19 pool. Of course I didnt complain at
the time, but is giving up and doing what is effectively walking away
legal during a tournament?

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Olivier_PEREZ wrote:
> Does that mean that people that it's illegal to transefer out when
> somone propose you 0.5 VP if you just accepte to not transfer out?

No, it's still legal. You're never obliged to trust someone to honor a deal.
But if there is the reasonable possibility of withdrawing or going to time, that
almost certainly means it is not play to win to play for less than 0.5 VPs, deal
or no deal.
